names.official: Macao Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China

summary: Macao runs its own liberal entry regime, separate from mainland China: EU and many other passports get 90 visa-free days (British citizens six months), dozens of nationalities get 30, and most of the rest can simply buy a visa on arrival at the border — only a handful of passports must apply in advance.

notes: The duty-free tobacco allowance is only 19 cigarettes — excess quantities are fined heavily.
E-cigarettes and vaping products may not be brought into Macao. They are prohibited items.

payments.text: Cards and mobile payments are accepted in casinos, hotels and malls, and Hong Kong dollars circulate 1:1 alongside the pataca. Keep some cash for street food, small shops and buses, and note patacas are hard to spend outside Macao.

safety.text: Macao has very low street crime and is comfortable to explore on foot at night. The usual cautions are typhoons in summer and keeping an eye on valuables in casino crowds.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Macao travel advice: safety and security

bestTimeToVisit.text: October to March brings cooler, drier weather ideal for the old town and Coloane; summer is hot, humid and prone to typhoons.

tips.text: Hong Kong dollars are accepted everywhere at 1:1 (casinos often prefer them), but change is usually given in patacas — spend your MOP before leaving, as they are almost impossible to exchange outside Macao.
Every arrival by ferry, bridge bus or air is a fresh entry with its own stay period — day-tripping from Hong Kong is easy, but frequent back-to-back visits to reset your stay will draw questions.
Macao's entry rules are separate from mainland China — crossing to Zhuhai through the Gongbei or Hengqin border needs a Chinese visa or an applicable mainland exemption, arranged separately.
During typhoon signal 8 or above (mostly June–October) ferries and the airport shut down and casinos may close. Check the SMG weather bureau signals in summer.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Macau?
faq.answer: Most travelers do not: EU and several dozen other passports enter visa-free for 90 days (British citizens for six months), and nationalities including the US, Canada, Australia, India and most of ASEAN get 30 days. Most remaining nationalities can buy a visa on arrival (MOP 200) at the border — only a handful, such as Bangladesh, Nepal, Nigeria, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Vietnam, must obtain a visa in advance through Chinese diplomatic missions.

faq.question: Is Macau covered by a Chinese visa?
faq.answer: No — Macao keeps its own immigration system. A mainland Chinese visa is not needed (or valid) for Macao, and Macao's visa-free entry gives no right to cross into Zhuhai or the rest of mainland China, which requires its own visa or exemption.

faq.question: How long can US citizens stay in Macau?
faq.answer: US passport holders enter visa-free for up to 30 days. EU citizens get 90 days, and British citizens up to six months, under Macao's more generous European arrangements.

faq.question: Can I do a day trip to Macau from Hong Kong?
faq.answer: Yes — ferries and the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge take about an hour, and immigration on both sides is quick for visa-free nationalities. Bring your passport: you formally exit Hong Kong and enter Macao, and each crossing uses a fresh entry stamp on both sides.

faq.question: How does the Macau visa on arrival work?
faq.answer: Eligible nationalities simply line up at the visa counter at the airport, ferry terminals or land border, pay MOP 200 (MOP 100 for children under 12) and receive a stay of up to 30 days on the spot; MOP 300 buys multiple entries within that stay. Nationalities excluded from the scheme must apply in advance through a Chinese embassy or consulate.
